cards.title: Equities: Gulf Risk Reaches Saudi Arabia's Investment Calendar
cards.body: The S&P 500 trades at {SPX} and the Nasdaq 100 at {NDX}. The war's clearest financial signal this week came from Riyadh, not New York: Saudi Arabia postponed its Future Investment Initiative, due 26–29 October, to 2027 because of Houthi strikes, and government agencies in Riyadh told staff to work from home. Oil, at {BRENT} for Brent, remains the main channel to equities. Supply risk sits in unconfirmed Houthi claims on Yanbu and Shaybah and continued ship attacks around Hormuz; relief sits in the US waiver of Russia sanctions and the IEA stock release.

cards.title: Oil: Prices Ease as Trump Plays Down New Iran Strikes
cards.body: Brent trades at {BRENT}. Brent ended last week near $98, its lowest in about a month, as Qatar's mediation and the end of the US midterms eased fears of a wider war. Trump's 9 November remark that further strikes on Iran are 'quite unlikely' points the same way. The blockade still holds, and US aircraft disabled a ship running it on 7 November. Houthi attacks on 8-9 November damaged an Aramco office tower in Riyadh and caused a limited fire on the East-West pipeline near Medina; Saudi Arabia said pipeline operations were unaffected. The pipeline is the main route around Hormuz, so a sustained outage would matter more than a strike headline.

cards.title: Crypto: Treasury Hits Iranian Money Rails in Canada and MEXC
cards.body: Bitcoin trades at {BTC}. On 6 November the US Treasury sanctioned eight Canadian money-exchange businesses it says moved Iranian funds, including the crypto firm Cryptoyal, and a separate Treasury release, read only by its title, says MEXC was cut off from the US financial system. That is a direct strike on payment rails Iran uses to move money around its blockade. Nothing new has been announced on the $6.3 billion Binance theft the FBI attributes to North Korea.

cards.title: Gold: Flat While Oil Swings
cards.body: Gold trades at {GOLD}. The last dated check this card holds: on 18 September gold was $4,364.46 an ounce at 9 a.m. New York time, against $4,364.63 a day earlier (CNBC). That is flat, in a week when Brent swung between the high $90s and above $107 on Saudi pipeline and Hormuz news, and it is still not safe-haven behaviour. The card's standing explanation holds: gold is being priced against real yields and the cost of holding it, not against the probability of escalation. A genuine flight to safety would show up in gold before it shows up in oil.
